title: Inquest tackles police shooting; Mother wants answers 16 months after her son died during a robbery
article: Karyn Graham will be on hand to hear every word when an coroner's inquest opens today into the death of her son Trevor.
But after waiting 16 months since he was shot and killed by police during a Kitchener drug store robbery, she still doesn't expect to get the answers she is looking for.
Graham already knows Trevor, 26, was a troubled, suicidal man wrestling with both an addiction to painkillers and mental-health issues.

She also realizes that Const. Laurie Cartwright probably went by the book when she pulled the trigger as Trevor -- stolen drugs in one hand and a knife-like object in the other -- kept coming at her despite demands to stop.

What she can't understand, or accept, is how he ended up at the Shoppers Drug Mart in the Sunrise Centre the night of Nov. 20, 2007, after a revolving door of run-ins with the law that never got at his underlying difficulties.
"When he became an adult, he wanted help and he tried to get it," she said. "But he just more or less gave up after he wasn't getting the right treatment from corrections."

Graham is frustrated after being told in the lead-up to the Kitchener inquest that it will focus primarily on the fatal shooting itself, not broader questions of how the justice and health systems deal with the mentally ill.
She plans to keep pushing for more communication between officials in those two systems and improved treatment programs in correctional facilities, particularly provincial jails.
"Unless we're allowed to look beyond the robbery and the shooting, we're not inquiring into the real cause," Graham said.
After struggling since adolescence, a turning point for Trevor came when he checked himself into a Hamilton hospital after a suicide attempt in late 2005.
Graham said it was going well until he went out to buy cigarettes and got arrested for breaching a court order to report to another facility for addictions treatment.
"It didn't make any sense to put him back into (jail), but that's what they did," she said.
During an armed, drunken standoff at his home in Paris, Ont., in the summer of 2007, Trevor slashed himself with a knife and urged two OPP officers to shoot him in the head.
That incident also landed him back in jail.
After his release, he came to live with his mother in Kitchener. He was shot in the chest during the robbery and died three days later.
A provincial watchdog agency found Cartwright acted reasonably.
The inquest -- mandatory under provincial law because Trevor died in police custody -- is expected to last two days and include testimony from about eight witnesses.
Dr. Jack Stanborough, the regional supervising coroner, will preside over the inquest.
